notes: Written from the maker's own source at commit 7dc3dab, "Update version and changelog", which is the commit that set the installed version 2.0.1; the nine commits after it in the repository still carry 2.0.1 but post-date the library release, and one of them changes ChowChorus filter behaviour at low sample rates, so they were deliberately not read. Also read: doc/manual.md in the same tree, the maker's own ChowTape plugin manual at chowdsp.com/manuals/ChowTapeManual.pdf for the five tape modules, and a render of every panel. Every number quoted in these entries is either a literal in that source or worked out from literals in it. Five modules carry an Oversampling submenu, which changes CPU cost and aliasing rather than the controls; the defaults are 4x on ChowTape and 2x on ChowDer, Werner and Warp. Four modules carry a Publication item that opens the paper the module implements. One conflict with the maker's own manual was found: the manual says ChowDer's Bass and Treble knobs drive a Baxandall EQ circuit, and in this version they drive a first-order shelving filter at 600Hz instead; the Baxandall wave digital filter is in the tree and compiled but never instantiated.

lines: A physical model of magnetic tape: the audio is driven through a Jiles-Atherton model of the tape's magnetic hysteresis, which is where tape distortion comes from
Sets the width of the hysteresis loop. At the left the loop is at its widest, which gives the dead band and the coarse distortion of underbiased tape, and turning it right closes the loop up.
Sets the level at which the tape saturates; turning it up brings the saturation point down, so the sound distorts sooner
Sets how hard the audio is driven into the hysteresis model, which changes the shape of the distortion rather than only its level
The audio to be put on tape; it is divided by 5 and clamped, so anything past 5V is already at the top of the model's range
The processed audio, at 4.18 times the model's own output
Note — the model runs at four times the sample rate when the module is added; the oversampling menu changes that.
Menu — Oversampling: 1x, 2x, 4x, 8x, 16x — sets how many times the internal sample rate is raised before the nonlinearity is computed; higher settings reduce aliasing and cost more CPU
Menu — Publication — opens the 2019 DAFx paper the tape model comes from in a web browser

ChowTape.notes: Read from the maker's source at commit 7dc3dab and from doc/manual.md in the same tree, with the control descriptions checked against the maker's own ChowTape plugin manual at chowdsp.com. The three knobs are all 0 to 1 with a default of 0.5 and the maker gave them no parameter names, so the panel lettering is the only name they have. In HysteresisProcessing::cook the saturation knob sets the saturation magnetisation as 1.5 minus the knob, the drive knob divides it by six times the drive, and the bias knob reaches the loop width as one minus the knob. The module builds a 30Hz DC blocking filter in process() and never calls it, so no DC blocking is applied; the output is the hysteresis output times 4.18.

The pre-delay knob runs 0 to 1 and is used as 500 raised to that power in milliseconds, so it is 1ms at the bottom, about 22ms at its default of 0.5 and 500ms at the top; the maker named the parameter Time and lettered the panel Pre-Delay. ChowRNN.notes: Read from the maker's source at commit 7dc3dab and doc/manual.md in the same tree. The four inputs carry no family colour: the manual says almost any signal can go in, and what the network makes of it depends on the weights, so nothing about a jack says what belongs there. The output layer's bias is zeroed at construction and a 30Hz high-pass follows the network. The randomise button is momentary and its parameter is read every sample, so holding it down rerolls the weights continuously.

ChowPulse.notes: Read from the maker's source at commit 7dc3dab and doc/manual.md in the same tree. The width knob is 0 to 1 used as 300 raised to that power in milliseconds and the decay knob as 30 raised to that power times ten milliseconds, both defaulting to 0.5, which is about 17ms and about 55ms. The decay time is turned into the two resistor values of the modelled circuit against a fixed 0.015 microfarad capacitor. The double tap knob is -1 to 1 and is used as minus twice its value, applied only where the shaped envelope is below zero, so at its centre the tail is removed entirely. None of the three CV inputs is clamped, so a large voltage can push a parameter far past what the knob can reach.

ChowTapeComp.notes: Read from the maker's source at commit 7dc3dab, doc/manual.md, and the maker's own ChowTape plugin manual at chowdsp.com, which is where the description of the amount control comes from. The attack and release times are exact: attack is 160000/9801 raised to the knob, times 9801/3010, minus 950/301, which is 0.1ms at the bottom and 50ms at the top; release is 100 raised to the knob times 10, which is 10ms to 1000ms. Both default to the middle of their knob, about 3.6ms and 100ms. The signal is divided by five before the level is measured and multiplied by five again on the way out, so the compression threshold is referred to a 5V peak.

ChowTapeDegrade.notes: Read from the maker's source at commit 7dc3dab, doc/manual.md, and the maker's own ChowTape plugin manual at chowdsp.com. All four knobs are 0 to 1 shown as a percentage and all four default to 0. In cookParams the filter frequency is 200Hz times 100 raised to one minus the amount knob, so amount at 0 leaves it at 20000Hz; the gain is -24dB times the depth knob; the noise gain is 0.33 times depth times amount, so both knobs have to be up for any noise. ChowTapeLoss.notes: Read from the maker's source at commit 7dc3dab, doc/manual.md, and the maker's own ChowTape plugin manual at chowdsp.com. Each knob is 0 to 1 with a default of 0.5 and an exponential display whose three constants are literals at the top of ChowTapeLoss.cpp; working the endpoints out gives gap 1 to 50, thickness 0.1 to 50, spacing 0.1 to 20, all in microns, and speed 1 to 50 inches per second. The maker's desktop manual gives spacing and thickness in centimetres and the gap in millimetres, but this module's own parameters are in microns and the code multiplies each by 1e-6 to reach metres. The filter is 64 taps at 44100Hz and longer in proportion at higher sample rates, rebuilt whenever a knob moves. The head bump is a peaking filter at the speed in metres per second divided by 500 times the gap, with a gain of at most 1.5.

lines: An ensemble chorus: four delay lines emulating a bucket-brigade chip, each swept by a slow and a fast sine, giving a stereo pair from a mono input
Sets how fast the sweeps run; the slow one moves between 0.005Hz and 5Hz and the fast one between 0.5Hz and 40Hz together
Sets how far the delays are swept, and so how deep the chorusing is
Sets how much of each channel's output is fed back into its delay lines, up to 0.39 of it; the feedback is high-passed at 240Hz so it cannot build up on the bass
Mixes the chorus against the dry signal, all dry at the left and all chorus at the right
The audio to be chorused; the same signal feeds both channels
One of the two channels; it carries the same input through two delay lines whose sweeps start a third of a cycle away from the other channel's
Note — the input is mono and the two outputs differ only in the starting phase of their sweeps, so one of them patched alone gives the chorus without the stereo spread.
Note — the module has no menu of its own beyond Rack's.

ChowChorus.notes: Read from the maker's source at commit 7dc3dab and doc/manual.md in the same tree. All four knobs are 0 to 1 shown as a percentage; rate, depth and mix default to the middle and feedback to zero. The rate knob is the exponent of both LFO sweeps at once, 0.005Hz to 5Hz for the slow pair and 0.5Hz to 40Hz for the fast pair. The feedback amount is 0.39 times the square root of the knob. Each channel runs two bucket-brigade delay lines of 4096 stages with a 12000Hz anti-aliasing filter after them and a 240Hz high-pass in the feedback path, and the four sweeps start at phases of minus a third of pi, zero, zero and a third of pi. The input is summed into the feedback through a hyperbolic tangent after being scaled by 0.075.
